title: 24/7 named-filer retainer for CRA reporting
one_liner: A follow-the-sun 'fractional PSIRT' that pre-registers, drills and files CRA Article 14 vulnerability reports on the ENISA portal for small connected-device makers.
customer: EU and non-EU manufacturers of connected products with roughly 5-250 staff and no 24/7 security team. Examples are smart-home, IP camera, e-bike and e-scooter electronics, EV charger, industrial IoT gateway, 3D printer and consumer robotics makers. Their CEO or head of product pays.
problem: Since 11 Sept 2026, manufacturers must send an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability, a fuller notice within 72 hours, and a final report later. This covers products already on the market, including 2019 models. Fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. The ENISA portal has no API at launch and needs 39 manual fields. Filers must be named individuals with EU Login and MFA. Picking the wrong coordinator CSIRT can invalidate a filing. The platform's 72-hour counter can show a compliant filing as overdue. Emailing a national CSIRT does not count. Small makers have no one awake on a Sunday who knows any of this.
solution: Sell a monthly retainer with four parts. (1) A pre-flight setup: named EU Login accounts, a documented coordinator-CSIRT choice, a product-to-Member-State map and the required vulnerability contact. (2) A one-page intake form and an 'awareness decision log' that keeps independent 24h/72h/14-day clocks and a defensible record of when the manufacturer became aware. (3) A rotating on-call engineer, holding one of the up-to-20 secondary filer seats under the manufacturer's written designation, who drafts and pastes the 39-field early warning within hours. (4) Twice-yearly tabletop drills that produce an audit-ready evidence file. The manufacturer stays legally responsible. We supply speed and process, not scanners.
why_now: Article 14 became binding on 11 Sept 2026 and the single reporting platform went live the same day. Registration guidance only started rolling out on 31 July. No CRA harmonised standard was in the Official Journal as of late August, and notified-body capacity is a 'best-efforts' December 2026 target. Small makers therefore have no standards shortcut and must run the reporting process by hand.
revenue_model: Setup fee of EUR 1,000-1,500. Retainer of EUR 250-600 per month by product count. Incident filing package of EUR 2-4k per event. Drill add-on of EUR 800. Later, referral or bundle deals with cyber insurers, notified-body consultants and contract manufacturers.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is a named human with a valid account, awake at 3am, making the 'awareness' judgment call. Scanner vendors are everywhere, but nobody sells the person and the drill. Evidence: the ENISA portal guide says 'Automate the preparation, not the filing' and lists no API, 39 fields, named-person accounts, the wrong-CSIRT risk and the misaligned 72h counter (https://craevidence.com/cra-compliance/enisa-srp-onboarding). An ENISA survey found 20% of SMEs were unsure the CRA even applied to them (https://www.techtarget.com/cybersecurity/feature/EU-Cyber-Resilience-Act-reporting-What-CISOs-need-to-know). Greenbone's readiness review found the platform still in testing two weeks before go-live and no standards published (https://www.greenbone.net/en/blog/cra-article-14-readiness-status/). ENISA launch note: https://www.enisa.europa.eu/news/the-cra-single-reporting-platform-is-launched.
first_30_days: Turn the public ENISA and Commission material into a free 'SRP pre-flight' checklist and a 24h/72h clock template, and publish both. Recruit 4-6 freelance product-security engineers across EU, US and Asia time zones for a rotation. Cold-message about 300 product-security, CE-compliance and CTO contacts at hardware makers (RED and CE registries, hardware crowdfunding lists). Offer 5 founding pilots at EUR 99 per month plus a free first drill. Book a tabletop drill with each pilot and convert the drill output into the case study.

title: Nonrenewal Cure: Rebutting Insurer Cancellations
one_liner: Nonrenewal notices often cite fixable issues like roof condition, tree overhang or debris. Sell homeowners a fast diagnosis, repair and evidence packet to get re-underwritten instead of dumped on a FAIR plan.
customer: Homeowners in CA, FL, TX, CO, UT and NM who have received a nonrenewal notice, plus independent brokers who lose those clients.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and homeowners have 30-75 days to react. Carriers are structurally conflicted about helping, and the FAIR plan is pricey with thin cover. Homeowners can't decode the reason code, can't tell which items are cheap to fix, and can't produce the evidence a carrier re-inspection accepts.
solution: Upload the notice. The service decodes the stated reason using state disclosure rules, dispatches vetted local contractors for the fix (patch, trim, vent screens), and produces a time-stamped photo and invoice packet. It files for reinspection or appeal, and gives the broker a clean file to re-market the risk. For wildfire-score cases it documents mitigation credits available under state rules.
why_now: Record nonrenewals, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03, and insurance now rivals mortgage payments. Carriers rely more on aerial-imagery flags that homeowners rarely see or contest.
revenue_model: $149 diagnostic, $250-$500 evidence packet, 10-15% contractor referral fee, and broker referral fees on re-placed policies.
non_obvious_insight: Many cancellations are cheap to cure, but the homeowner has no language, time or evidence, and the carrier won't help. A homeowner who has just been rescued becomes a lifetime referral source for brokers.
first_30_days: Post in local nonrenewal threads and neighborhood groups, and partner with three independent brokers. Handle 20 cases by hand, track how many carriers reinstate, and use the win rate to set pricing.

title: Rescue Orphaned Steno Notes With Stroke-Level AI
one_liner: A translation service that turns retired or deceased reporters' unreadable steno files into certifiable transcripts for stalled appeals, using a neural stroke-to-text model in place of the missing personal dictionary.
customer: County and state court administrators, public defender and appellate defender offices, and state AG appellate divisions. Secondary customers are retiring reporters and their estates. The first buyer is an appellate defender office with transcript orders stuck because the reporter left, paying about $2.50-$4 per page with a $1,500 minimum.
problem: Steno notes are a personal code, not a shared language. Another reporter cannot read them without the writer's dictionary, which holds phonetic strokes plus thousands of private shortcuts called briefs. When a reporter retires, dies or moves away, their untranscribed notes are effectively dead. Appeals stall for months, and courts may have to redo hearings or accept an inadequate record. Retention rules (California is 10 years for criminal cases and 5 for most others) mean old notes are also being boxed up or destroyed as reporters retire. The average reporter is in their mid-50s, and the workforce has shrunk about 21% in a decade.
solution: Train a stroke-sequence model. Input is the raw stroke stream with timestamps. Output is English with punctuation and Q/A structure. Training data comes from open steno corpora and community theory dictionaries, synthetic strokes with randomized personal-brief variation, and consented archives from retired reporters. Where the reporter also ran a backup audio recording, fuse audio and strokes to resolve homophones. Sell three products. (1) Rescue: per-page conversion, human-scoped by a retired reporter who certifies the transcript as prepared from the original reporter's notes. (2) Archive escrow: retiring reporters pay a one-time fee or a small monthly fee to have notes and dictionary converted, indexed and held by a custodian that satisfies retention rules. (3) Later, a scoping copilot for active reporters, who spend 1-3 hours editing per hour of testimony.
why_now: The 2026 retirement wave is here, and NCRA-cited data puts the average member age around 56. The 5-10 year retention windows for notes written in 2016-2021 are closing now. California's 2026 Supreme Court ruling (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) requires courts to give indigent litigants a verbatim record on request, which will create more appeals that need transcripts. Sequence models can now handle noisy phonetic-to-text conversion with context, and the open steno community (Plover) has published theory and dictionaries.
revenue_model: Per-page rescue fees, priced below the $4-6 ordinary transcript rate and paid by courts or appellate offices. Escrow and conversion packages for retirees (about $300-$800 one-time, or $25 per month). Annual contracts with court systems for backlog clearing. Later, a $99-$149 per month scoping copilot for active reporters, who already pay $3,000+ for CAT software.
non_obvious_insight: Only the writer can read steno notes. Court administrators do not track how many untranscribed notes sit with reporters about to retire. The stroke stream is also a cleaner input than audio, because a trained human already resolved the speaker, punctuation and homophones in real time. Almost nobody outside the profession knows the raw-notes problem exists.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 retired reporters through state association retiree lists. They donate or license old practice files and act as reviewers and certifiers. Build a baseline model on synthetic and open steno data, then test it blind on their files and record the accuracy. Cold-call 10 appellate defender and public defender offices with one question: do you have appeals stalled because the reporter is unavailable? Close 2-3 paid pilots at the $1,500 minimum.

title: Exit Desk for Orphaned Local-Marketing Assets
one_liner: A fixed-price service that finds, takes back and migrates the domain, listing, phone numbers and ad accounts locked inside shrinking legacy marketing vendors.
customer: Home-service and retail owners paying $200-1,200 a month to Yellow Pages descendants, marketing agencies and template-site hosts.
problem: Thryv's 2025 revenue was $785M and falling, with net income near $0.3M, so the vendor base is melting through price hikes, resales and shutdowns. Owners often do not own their domain, Google Business Profile admin rights, call-tracking numbers or ad accounts, and leaving means losing the phone number painted on the truck. Getting customers is still the top small-business challenge.
solution: A fixed-fee audit finds recurring vendor debits (via bank feed or bookkeeper), checks who owns each asset (WHOIS, GBP owner list, ad-account admin, tracking numbers), then executes the takeback: domain transfer, GBP ownership transfer, number port, site migration into an owner-owned stack, and contract cancellation notices. Optional monitoring alerts if a vendor re-takes control.
why_now: Legacy vendor decline is visible in public financials, AI site builders make replacement stacks cheap, and small businesses still need customers.
revenue_model: $299-799 one-time, $29/month monitoring, and referral fees from the destination stack (hosting, CRM, review tools).
non_obvious_insight: What the owner is paying for is a person who answers the phone, not leads. The exit is a control and trust problem more than a marketing problem. The bookkeeper sees the debit but has no workflow to end it.
first_30_days: Partner with 10 bookkeepers to flag legacy-vendor debits. Run 20 audits and publish a 'who owns your phone number' checklist to seed leads.

title: A Marketplace for Canal Capacity, Not Water
one_liner: A scheduling and capacity-release board that lets irrigation districts sell idle canal and wheeling capacity so conserved or recharge water can physically move to buyers.
customer: Irrigation districts and mutual ditch companies with spare conveyance capacity (sellers), plus growers, groundwater agencies, cities and conservation buyers who need water moved (buyers). Districts pay a subscription and buyers pay per acre-foot wheeled.
problem: Everyone is building marketplaces for water rights and acre-feet. In Western practice the binding constraint is often the ability and permission to move water: capacity, wheeling agreements, losses, turnout scheduling. Idle capacity sits unused while buyers cannot get water delivered. Districts handle wheeling requests by phone and spreadsheet.
solution: Wedge: a shared capacity calendar and wheeling-request workflow for districts, with loss accounting and standard agreements. Then a capacity-release market, like the gas-pipeline capacity release model. The ditch-company share ledger (shares, assessments, transfer approvals) is phase two. Start with one region where transfers already happen.
why_now: The 2027-2036 Colorado River framework and corporate buyers like Amazon create conserved water that must be moved. California groundwater rules and canal capacity loss to subsidence make wheeling scarce. Cheap LoRa gate sensors and open flow gauges make district digitization affordable.
revenue_model: $10-40k/yr district SaaS, plus $5-15 per acre-foot wheeled (roughly 3-5% of price).
non_obvious_insight: Price discovery is missing for the pipes, not the water. Whoever runs the capacity ledger sees every buyer, seller and route, and that data is the moat for every later water market product.
first_30_days: Interview 10 district managers and ditch riders and find one that handles recurring wheeling requests manually. Ship a free shared calendar and request workflow to that district using off-the-shelf tools. Agree that the district will pay per wheeled acre-foot at season end. Publish a public canal-capacity map from open gauge data as top-of-funnel.

title: Prospecting for Brackish Aquifers Like Gold
one_liner: A water-exploration company that maps, options and permits high-yield brackish and fresh aquifers before developers need them, then sells or leases 'water-ready' sites and supply.
customer: Data-center developers, small towns and rural districts, ranchers and industrial parks needing 1-5 MGD of defensible supply. Buyers pay for studies, and later for site options and supply contracts.
problem: About 1,800 ERCOT projects are held, and water is the new gating item. Siting decisions are still made on power and fiber first, and water studies come late from generalist consultants. Groundwater in Texas is private property under the rule of capture subject to local district rules (my understanding), so early options on proven supply are valuable, yet almost nobody is exploring for water the way miners explore for minerals.
solution: Use public airborne-electromagnetic surveys, well logs and machine learning to map the probability of high-yield brackish aquifers. Option land and water rights, drill test wells, obtain production permits, and pair with a treatment partner. Sell paid site reports first, then options and long-term supply.
why_now: Drone-borne electromagnetic surveys are getting cheap, brackish desalination costs are falling, and regulators are blocking new load without a proven water plan.
revenue_model: $15-75k paid site studies, drilling programs on cost-plus or success fee, and $1-5M site-option or supply sales.
non_obvious_insight: Water rights are the new mineral rights. The geophysics is becoming a commodity, but the permitting playbook and early option positions are not.
first_30_days: Sell five 'water-ready screening' reports at $15-25k to developers in the ERCOT queue and to towns, using public data only. Line up a drilling partner and identify two parcels near transmission with promising brackish aquifers to option.

title: CJIS 6.0 Identity Kit for Small Agencies
one_liner: A managed multifactor and identity-verification stack that works in patrol cars, radio dead zones and shared workstations, ready for the Oct 1, 2027 CJIS deadline.
customer: Sheriff's offices and police departments with 10-150 sworn officers and no dedicated IT security staff, plus the managed service providers that serve them.
problem: CJIS 6.0 requires MFA and identity verification by Oct 1, 2027. Generic MFA breaks on shared terminals, offline vehicles and old mobile data computers. Small agencies buy compliance piecemeal from a few vendors and fail audits.
solution: Hardware keys plus a cached-token offline mode and a shared-workstation login flow, with an agency-level compliance dashboard and audit-ready evidence. Onboard officers in minutes through mobile driver's license or badge-based identity proofing.
why_now: The deadline is fixed and less than 13 months out. Agencies are starting budget cycles now, and state CJIS systems agencies will begin enforcing.
revenue_model: $8-15 per user per month or a per-agency package of $6-30K per year, plus hardware sold at cost plus margin.
non_obvious_insight: The real customer is the MSP serving 50 small agencies. One channel partner delivers dozens of deployments, and offline behavior is the differentiator that enterprise identity vendors will not build.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 MSPs that serve sheriffs. Prototype offline token caching on a rugged laptop. Run 3 no-cost pilots in agencies with upcoming CJIS audits.

title: Hidden Satellite Tags Against Fictitious Pickups
angle: Pairing 2: Space economy x Cybersecurity/identity fraud (business scams and identity theft)
one_liner: A cargo custody kit that pairs a verified-carrier check at pickup with several disposable Bluetooth-to-satellite tags hidden in each load, giving brokers and insurers evidence of where freight went when it was stolen.
customer: Mid-size freight brokers (20-200 staff) and 3PLs moving theft-prone loads (electronics, pharma, beverages, copper) on US and cross-border lanes, and inland-marine cargo insurers or MGAs that have raised deductibles on theft. Start with brokers hit by fictitious pickups.
problem: Thieves impersonate legitimate carriers and dispatchers (increasingly with cloned voices), pick up loads and vanish. The one expensive GPS tracker per trailer is found and jammed, cell-based devices fail in remote drop points, and the broker learns hours later. Paperwork chains are spoofable, and insurers cannot prove the exact custody break.
solution: (1) An identity gate at pickup that partners with existing carrier-verification vendors (MC/DOT match, live driver ID, verified call-back). (2) Three to five disposable $5-12 Bluetooth-to-satellite tags bound to the bill of lading at pickup and hidden in cartons. (3) An evidence timeline of last-seen sightings from orbit, including where there is no cell coverage, compared against the declared route. (4) Police-ready location packets and an insurer-accepted custody report that earns premium credits.
why_now: Bluetooth-to-satellite just crossed into serious capital: Hubble Network raised a $200M Series C at a $1.6B valuation on 28 Sept 2026, with 6 satellites up and a next generation in 2027 aiming at much lower-power detection. Cheaper launch is collapsing per-tag and per-message costs. Voice-clone impersonation and business email compromise ($3.05B in US losses) make carrier identity fraud easier.
revenue_model: $12-25 per protected load with volume tiers, an insurer revenue share on premium credits, and annual platform fees for brokers with more than 5,000 loads.
non_obvious_insight: Trackers fail because thieves can find and defeat the single expensive device. When a tag costs $6 and needs no phone network, a broker can hide many of them, and abundance beats stealth. Current sat-BLE revisit times are hours, so the product is priced as last-seen evidence and recovery, not live tracking. The true buyer is often the insurer, who values proof of the custody-break moment.
first_30_days: Buy 500 tags through the vendor developer program. Recruit 3 brokers via freight-intermediary association networks. Tag every load on their two highest-theft lanes at cost for 30 days and log coverage and gaps. Bring the results to two cargo MGAs and negotiate a premium-credit pilot.

title: Independent audit desk for city surveillance vendors
one_liner: A fixed-price monthly service that checks whether a city's license-plate-reader and drone vendor is actually following the city's own sharing rules, and hands the council a report it can cite.
customer: City auditors, city attorneys and city managers (plus police oversight boards) in the roughly 50+ cities that cancelled or suspended Flock and the many more that kept ALPR or drone programs under new council conditions. Buyers pay $1.2k-2.5k/month per city from the auditor, city attorney or IT budget, well under the informal-procurement threshold.
problem: Cities cannot verify what the surveillance vendor does with their data. Mountain View's own audit found a statewide-lookup setting active on 29 of 30 cameras since program start, with 250+ outside agencies running about 600,000 searches in 12 months, and the vendor kept no records that would show what was shared. Oxnard's vendor silently re-enabled a nationwide query feature. Evanston found cameras reinstalled after cancellation. Dayton found 7,100+ searches for immigration enforcement that city policy prohibited. Councils now write audit duties into ordinances, but the auditor's office has no tooling.
solution: A vendor-neutral audit service (Flock, Axon, Motorola/Vigilant, drone platforms). The city exports the search and audit logs and sharing-settings screenshots it can already download. The service ingests them and runs a rules engine against the city's adopted policy: searches with no case number or with vague reason codes, out-of-state or federal agencies, immigration-related terms, off-hours spikes, and diffs of the network-sharing settings month to month to catch silent config changes. Output is a council-ready quarterly report and a same-week alert on config drift. Add-on: a field check that cameras a council ordered off are really off, since Evanston found them reinstalled.
why_now: 53 cities across 20 states had cancelled or rejected Flock by mid-2026 over unauthorized federal access. New state laws (Colorado SB 26-070 warrant rule, Washington SB 6002, Kentucky HB 58 90-day retention cap, Maine's ALPR law) add compliance duties. Atlanta's ordinance, held in committee and taken up again in September 2026, would require monthly internal access audits and annual independent technical audits managed by the City Auditor. Drone-as-first-responder approvals (Stockton, Federal Way, Santa Fe, Whittier) are expanding the audit surface.
revenue_model: $4.5k one-time baseline configuration and log audit, then $1.2k-2.5k/month monitoring and quarterly council report. Upsell: annual independent technical audit that ordinances like Atlanta's require, priced $15k-40k for larger cities. Multi-year contracts through city auditor offices.
non_obvious_insight: The market is created by oversight ordinances, not by the surveillance vendors. Every ordinance that says 'audit monthly' is an unfunded mandate on a three-person auditor's office, and the failure mode is configuration drift, not sophisticated data science. Evidence: Mountain View's statewide lookup ran from launch until Jan 5, 2026 unnoticed (https://www.mv-voice.com/police/2026/01/30/amid-immigration-crackdown-mountain-view-discovers-unauthorized-access-to-license-plate-data/). The audit findings and 53-city cancellation count are in https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319317/20260629/flock-safety-crosses-100000-cameras-53-cities-cancel-over-unauthorized-federal-data-access.htm. Atlanta's proposed monthly internal and annual independent audits are at https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2026/09/22/atlanta-weighs-sweeping-rules-monthly-audits-surveillance-tech/. New Hanover County's commissioners called for 'explicit guardrails' before restoring cameras: https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9840468/north-carolina/new-hanover-county/commissioners-cite-privacy-shifting-vendor-policies-and-misuse-when-cancelling-flock-alpr-contract. Cities that keep the cameras need proof of compliance to survive the next council vote, and the audit report is that proof.
first_30_days: File public-records requests in about 25 cities that cancelled or kept ALPR for the audit-log export format and sharing-settings history, and build a parser for it. Produce one free 'configuration drift' teardown for a friendly city attorney or a councilmember who championed the cancellation. Pitch the $4.5k baseline audit to auditors and attorneys in cities with surveillance-oversight ordinances (Seattle, San Diego, Oakland, Cambridge, Urbana) and to those now drafting them (Atlanta). Sign 3 pilots. Main risk: vendor cooperation and export formats, so start with cities that already run their own audits.

title: Mailed Proof Books for Grandparents Who Buy Prints
one_liner: Turn a wedding gallery into a personalized printed booklet, mailed to each grandparent and parent with a phone number to order prints, because the people who actually pay for wedding prints never click gallery links.
customer: Wedding photographers (they pay only via revenue share). The end payers are the couple's parents, in-laws and grandparents, who spend $150-400 per household on prints and albums.
problem: The dirty secret of studio economics is that couples buy almost nothing after delivery. They have the gallery and Instagram. The people who buy prints and albums are mothers, mothers-in-law and grandparents, and the photographer's only delivery channel is a link emailed to the couple, who rarely forward it. Pic-Time and similar platforms added face-recognition and selfie-search galleries in late 2025, but that assumes a phone-comfortable guest willing to scan their face on a website. Grandma will not do that. Every wedding leaves an estimated $500-2,000 of print revenue uncollected, and the 'last photo with Grandpa' has a clock on it.
solution: The photographer uploads the gallery and the family list (they already have it from the formals shot list). We cluster faces, have the photographer confirm the 6-12 key elders and parents, and auto-build a 16-24 page softcover booklet per person ('Nana's Book: 22 photos of you and your grandkids'). We print and mail it within about 10 days of gallery delivery, with the couple's opt-in and a handwritten-style note from them. Every booklet carries a QR code plus a toll-free number answered first by a human and later by a voice agent that takes orders by phone and card, with check-by-mail as an option. Orders are fulfilled through pro labs, and the photographer sees a dashboard of sales.
why_now: AI face search has just become standard in photographer gallery platforms (Pic-Time's Nov 2025 update), which proves photographers will pay for AI galleries but leaves the elder channel unserved. Softcover print-on-demand now lands at roughly $6-10 for a 24-page book via lab and POD APIs. 2026-grade voice agents can take a print order from a 78-year-old who hates websites. Wedding-guest demographics are also aging, since couples are marrying later and grandparents are still at the table.
revenue_model: No upfront fee to the photographer. We front the booklet cost (about $10 landed) and keep roughly 40% of resulting print and album order revenue at lab retail, with the photographer keeping 60%, which is pure incremental margin. Optional $15 flat per-booklet pricing for photographers who want to buy outright.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the client. The couple's inbox is the wrong channel, and a personalized object with the recipient's own face on it is something people do not throw away. The product is a channel to 60-85-year-olds who respond to paper and phone calls, and the gallery software is just the data source.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 photographers from local and online groups who delivered a wedding in the last 6 months. Produce booklets for 2 of their weddings each, at your cost (about $100 in print and postage per wedding), using a Pic-Time/ShootProof export, open-source face clustering (InsightFace) and a lab or Lulu/Blurb-style API. Route the phone number to the founder's cell. Track orders per booklet. If 1 in 5 booklets converts to a $100+ order, sign the rev-share terms and scale to 50 studios.

title: Cask Audit: Proof of Existence for Whisky Investors
one_liner: An independent inspection, gauging and valuation service that verifies investor-owned whisky casks exist, contain what was sold, and are worth what the seller says.
customer: Retail cask investors, IFAs and wealth managers, insolvency practitioners and law firms, and honest cask brokers who want a trust seal.
problem: The cask market has been in a glut since 2022 (auction surplus, distillery consolidation, lower price per litre) and has documented fraud cases where audits found casks missing or filled with substandard spirit. Investors cannot verify holdings or exit.
solution: Field inspectors in bonded warehouses attest existence, fill level, strength, cask type and warehouse-receipt ownership, with geotagged photos. Quarterly valuations use bottling yield and market comps, and brokers pay to join an 'audited cask' registry.
why_now: In a downturn demand shifts from buying more to proving what you own. Fraud taints every honest broker, so third-party proof is worth paying for.
revenue_model: GBP 150-300 per cask audit, broker subscriptions for continuous audit, and valuation reports.
non_obvious_insight: Bonded-warehouse access is already a contractual owner right, so inspectors are cheap to deploy, while buyers of proof are motivated by loss and by seller reputation. The bourbon cask market is a later expansion. Confirm warehouse cooperation and local regulation early.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 warehouse-keepers, audit 30 casks for 10 investors at a GBP 100 pilot rate, publish anonymized findings, and approach IFAs and insolvency firms.

title: Vet-Supervised Cattle Crews for the Screwworm Era
one_liner: Custom-harvester-style crews do the 80% of a vet's working day that is labor (inspect, treat navels, tag, record) so the scarce vet supervises and signs instead of holding the chute.
customer: Ranchers in screwworm zones and buffer states (Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma) paying per head or per day; sale barns, stocker operations and feedlots that need pre-movement inspection documentation; and overloaded rural vet practices that subcontract overflow to a crew.
problem: Only about 1.3% of vets work in food animal practice, and South Texas vets say it will not be physically possible to handle every screwworm case. Daily inspection is the core control, newborn calves' navels are prime targets (past outbreaks saw navel strike rates as high as 50% in unprotected calves), and ranchers with 300-3,000 head across brush country do not have the labor to look at every animal every day.
solution: A vet-supervised service company (a rural vet as medical director, or a vet-owned entity) fielding 3-4 person crews with a trailer: portable squeeze chute, EID reader, wound-care kit, vet-approved treatment protocols, and a photo- and GPS-stamped inspection log that the vet countersigns. The seasonal product is an 'NWS Season Program' of scheduled pasture rounds, navel treatment on newborn calves, wound checks, prescribed prophylactic treatments under an existing VCPR, and movement paperwork. Off-season the same crews run preg-checks, weaning, vaccination and processing days year-round, with the vet doing exams and sign-off.
why_now: The first US screwworm detections came in Texas in June 2026, followed by more counties, a New Mexico detection, and the first infested horse in September. Sterile fly supply is constrained, federal and state agencies have imposed movement restrictions and mandatory veterinary inspections in affected areas, and FDA has moved to authorize treatment products. Spring calving in Texas is the next high-risk window.
revenue_model: $3-8 per head per treatment or round, day rates around $1,800-2,500 per crew for working days, seasonal retainer contracts, and a 20-30% margin on subcontracted overflow from vet practices. Target roughly 35-40% gross margin per crew.
non_obvious_insight: The vet shortage is largely a labor-allocation problem: a $250-per-hour license is spent on tasks that only need hands. Custom crews are normal for harvest, hay and branding, but herd health stayed in-house because vets never delegated it formally. Practice-of-veterinary-medicine laws let a supervising vet delegate many tasks, and once the vet is medical director of record the boundary is workable. The durable asset is the trained crew that keeps earning long after screwworm fades, because labor-short ranches will keep buying it.
first_30_days: Sign 2 overloaded vets in Texas or New Mexico as medical directors, and confirm what each state's practice act allows non-vets to do. Buy a used portable chute, trailer and 2 EID readers (about $15K), recruit 3 experienced ranch hands or vet-tech students, and get liability coverage. Sell 5 ranches a fall program of weaning-time inspections and navel and wound checks on fall-calving herds, then sell the spring calving program from the results.

title: Waiver-Funded Home Modification Back Office and Factoring
one_liner: Handle the prior-authorization paperwork and advance payment for small contractors who do ramps and bathroom retrofits funded by Medicaid waivers and VA grants.
customer: Small accessibility and remodeling contractors (3-15 employees) in states with waiver home-modification benefits, plus case managers and AAAs who can't find bidders.
problem: Senior housing supply is stuck through 2030, so aging in place is structurally favored and home mods are the cheapest fix. But waiver and VA HISA funding needs OT assessments, multiple bids, packets, inspections and 60-120 day payment, so good contractors avoid it. Approved seniors can't find anyone to do the work.
solution: A back office that prepares the packet (OT evaluation scheduling, standard scope, photos, bids, permits), tracks approval, submits invoices, and advances 85-90% of payment within five days against the approved authorization. A network directory shows case managers which contractors are ready to bid.
why_now: 41 states have HCBS waitlists over 600k, so states favor cheap home-based solutions over $115k-a-year nursing home stays. Medicaid cuts and 15-month waits add pressure, while 80+ growth means demand for mods is up.
revenue_model: 3-5% packet fee, a 1.5-3% factoring spread, and a platform fee from states or MCOs for a ready-to-bid contractor pool.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for funded home modifications is contractor cash flow and paperwork, not consumer demand or budget. Fixing the contractor's experience creates supply where the money already exists.
first_30_days: In one state, recruit five contractors and process 10 packets. Secure a small credit line from a CDFI or SBA lender to fund advances, then approach the state's HCBS case management office.

title: Verified Gig Work History via Data-Access Rights
one_liner: Use statutory data-access requests as an API to pull couriers' and drivers' records from platforms, and issue a verified work-history credential they can carry to landlords, lenders and rival platforms.
customer: Couriers, ride-hail drivers, hosts and cleaners in the EU and UK are the users. Payers are letting agents and landlords, credit unions, neobanks and car-leasing firms verifying variable income, and platforms new to a city that want to import proven riders.
problem: Gig income and ratings are locked in platform apps. Screenshots are unverifiable, so lenders and landlords reject workers or demand guarantors. Changing platforms resets reputation to zero, and deactivations are opaque.
solution: An Export Desk. The worker signs a mandate. The service files GDPR access and portability requests to each platform (and requests under the Platform Work Directive as national laws land), normalizes the data into a standard schema, cross-checks it against bank statements, and issues a signed Work History Credential. It carries tenure, 12-month net income with variance, rating percentile, hours and deactivation events, and it can be shared by link or QR with selective disclosure. Pooled volume gives workers a bargaining bloc.
why_now: The EU Platform Work Directive must be transposed by 2 December 2026, and the Commission says no delay is possible. It strengthens workers' rights to information about algorithmic management. Italy has a draft law, Germany and Spain are moving, and the data-access rights already exist under GDPR and UK GDPR.
revenue_model: Free for workers. Lenders and letting agents pay $6-15 per verified pack, new-entrant platforms pay $20-40 per imported worker, and workers can pay about $4 a month for auto-refresh.
non_obvious_insight: When platforms will not offer an API, the statute is the API. Response clocks are slow but predictable. Once thousands of workers use it, platforms will want to build real APIs to avoid processing requests, and you become the neutral verifier they must integrate with.
first_30_days: Partner with a couriers' or drivers' union or a worker-data nonprofit. Onboard 100 couriers in London or Amsterdam. Produce 50 verified packs by filing requests and reconciling with bank data. Sign two letting agents or a credit union to accept the packs as an alternative to guarantors for a pilot.

title: Paid Holds: Options Market for Booking Agents
one_liner: A merchant plugin that sells time-limited holds on appointments, tables and inventory to shopping and booking agents, so agent traffic becomes fee revenue for the merchant instead of something to block.
customer: Wallet-holding consumer assistant agents and browser agents, which pay through AP2, ACP or Stripe/Tempo MPP rails. Supply side is independent restaurants, salons, dentists, physios, tee-time, boat and experience operators on Acuity, Square Appointments, Booksy, Cal.com or Mindbody.
problem: Agents shop in parallel. One errand fans out to 20-50 merchants and the agent wants to keep the best option open until its principal approves. Free holds are free options, so merchants see phantom demand, no-show slots and sold-out tables. Their response is to block agents: eBay barred buy-for-me agents in Feb 2026 and Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent on 22 Sept 2026.
solution: The merchant sets a hold price (for example 2-5% of ticket value, $1 minimum) and a duration (10 minutes to 24 hours). The agent calls hold(), pays programmatically and gets a signed hold receipt the merchant honors. If the agent converts, the fee is credited to the booking. If not, the merchant keeps it and we take 25%. The service also dedupes so retrying agents don't double-book. Later, hold prices float with demand, giving each slot an implied option value.
why_now: Google's AP2 v0.2 added human-not-present payments and moved to the FIDO Alliance. Stripe and Tempo's Machine Payments Protocol went live in March 2026, and Visa and Mastercard both have agent rails. Merchants are blocking agents right now, and the Ninth Circuit vacated Amazon's injunction against Perplexity in Aug 2026, so blocking is legally shaky. Visa expects millions of agent-made purchases this holiday season.
revenue_model: 25% of hold fees, plus a 1-2% referral fee on converted bookings. The merchant plugin is free to install. Later, a paid demand-analytics dashboard for merchants showing agent search intent by slot.
non_obvious_insight: Merchants are not hostile to agents. They are hostile to free options. Agents are the first buyers rational enough to price optionality, so charging for holds turns an adversarial scraping problem into a market. Airlines already sell fare holds, so the concept is proven with humans. Agents make it viable at $1 scale, and the hold price becomes a demand signal merchants have never had.
first_30_days: Build on the public webhooks and APIs of Cal.com, Acuity and Square Appointments. Recruit about 40 independent salons, barbers and physios in one metro with a free plugin, paying them out of our own test agents' wallets. Ship an MCP server exposing hold_and_book. Get 3 consumer-agent or browser-agent builders to integrate through x402/MPP hackathons. Measure hold-to-book conversion and no-show reduction, then charge live fees in months 2-3.

title: Contingency Collection for Small-Claims Winners
one_liner: Post-judgment enforcement for the $500-$10k creditor who won in court but cannot collect: skip-trace, levy and garnishment paperwork done for a percentage.
customer: Small landlords with unpaid-rent or damage judgments, tenants with deposit judgments, freelancers and contractor-fraud victims, paying a $99 setup plus 25-30% of dollars actually recovered.
problem: Roughly 70-80% of civil and small-claims judgments go uncollected, and the winner must find assets and file every enforcement step alone. Enforcement costs can exceed the judgment, tenants disappear without forwarding addresses, and attorneys skip small cases. Cheap filing tools like trysmallclaims ($149 demand letter, $299 filing) stop at judgment.
solution: Automate post-judgment work: skip-trace the debtor, discover employer and bank via debtor-exam forms, e-file state-specific wage garnishment and bank levy packets, schedule sheriff or constable levies, and calendar renewals and follow-ups. A partner licensed collection agency or attorney in each state handles regulatory compliance. Offer a pre-filing 'collectability score' so creditors learn whether the defendant has a job or bank account before spending on court.
why_now: Self-serve filing tools are creating more small-claims judgments, while enforcement remains manual and state-specific. Consumer data APIs and LLM document drafting make per-state packets cheap, and small landlords face rising unpaid-rent losses and slow evictions, so many are holding judgments they cannot collect.
revenue_model: 25-30% contingency on recovered dollars, $99 setup fee, and a $19 collectability score for pre-filing triage; later B2B seats for landlord associations and property managers.
non_obvious_insight: A widely cited split says about 20% of debtors pay voluntarily, 60% are 'strategic avoiders' who have assets but make the creditor work, and 20% are judgment-proof (https://www.trysmallclaims.com/blog/small-claims-court-judgment-enforcement-tools-by-state). The middle 60% is a repeatable, automatable playbook, and the competitor sells only filing and demand letters. The ABA Journal notes about 80% of civil money judgments remain unenforced and that only 3 of the top 50 law schools teach judgment enforcement (https://www.abajournal.com/voice/article/why-do-80-of-judgments-remain-uncollected). Landlord-side friction is described at https://www.fastevictionservice.com/blog/why-small-claims-court-judgments-are-hard-to-enforce/, which notes costs 'sometimes exceeding the amount of the judgment itself'. Reddit was unreachable, so the r/Landlord and r/legaladvice 'I won, now how do I collect?' pattern is inferred from these secondary sources.
first_30_days: Pick California or Texas. Approach two local apartment or landlord associations and collect 10-20 existing unpaid judgments on contingency. Sign a licensed collection agency or attorney partner, build the skip-trace plus writ and levy templates for one county, run garnishments manually first, and publish recovery statistics after the first 5 collections.

title: Snow Mutual: Weather Swaps Between Opposite Businesses
one_liner: A peer-to-peer weather-swap exchange that nets opposite snowfall exposures inside a metro, matching per-push plow operators with seasonal-flat operators and per-push property managers so no one pays insurer-grade premiums.
customer: Independent snow-plow and landscaping contractors (10-200 trucks) and small commercial property managers, HOAs and retail owners in Great Lakes and Northeast snowbelts.
problem: Snow contracts are weather bets. A dry winter crushes per-push operators' revenue while truck notes, insurance and retainer labor stay fixed. A heavy winter blows up seasonal-flat operators' costs and property managers' per-push budgets. Traditional insurance for this is thin and expensive, so nearly everyone is unhedged.
solution: Standardized index contracts, either seasonal snowfall or count of 2+ inch events at a named NWS/airport station. They are matched inside a metro. The platform holds collateral, nets opposing positions and lays off only the residual to a reinsurer or weather-derivative desk. Onboarding asks for your contract mix and returns a 'snow exposure score' and a suggested swap. Version one is an index-linked price-collar clause in the service contract itself, which needs no insurance license. A licensed MGA structure follows.
why_now: NOAA CPC/IRI's September 2026 outlooks put a greater than 90% chance on a very strong El Niño this winter, and seasonal snowfall maps lean below normal for the Great Lakes and Northeast, with lake-effect still a wildcard. Sentiment is lopsided and uncertain. Renewals and pricing decisions happen between now and November, so contractors are actively thinking about winter risk.
revenue_model: A fee of 8-12% of matched notional, charged to both sides, plus a small annual membership. Later, a margin on the unmatched residual layer and reinsurance placement fees.
non_obvious_insight: The snow industry already contains natural hedgers on both sides of every winter. Operators with per-push books and operators with seasonal-flat books have opposite exposures, and so do property managers. The need is mostly a matching problem, and matching removes the capital cost that makes small-business weather cover uneconomic.
first_30_days: Recruit through snow-industry associations, plow-forum groups and property-management associations. Sign about 15 operators and 15 property managers in one metro. Draft the index-collar addendum with a commercial lawyer and run a pilot on winter 2026-27 contracts with small capped notionals. Line up an MGA and a reinsurance quote for the residual.

title: ZIP-Level Appetite Radar for Distressed Markets
one_liner: A live map of which carriers are actually binding homes in which distressed ZIPs, sold to agents and to carriers owing coverage quotas.
customer: Independent agents and wholesale brokers in California (then Florida and Colorado). Carriers pay for pre-qualified submissions in ZIPs where they owe quota.
problem: The CA FAIR Plan hit 696,562 policies (up 8% since Sept 2025) and raised rates about 29.1%. Under the Sustainable Insurance Strategy, carriers get rate freedom in exchange for an 85% writing commitment in distressed ZIPs. Zurich, Mercury and CSAA say they are expanding, yet the June 2026 regulator release gave no numbers. Agents burn hours on declines, and nobody can see the ZIP-by-ZIP flip.
solution: Combine agent-contributed anonymized quote outcomes, licensed quote probing and rate/rule filing monitoring. Publish which carriers bind in each ZIP by roof age and mitigation class, with estimated savings versus FAIR. Agents get a 'who will write this' answer in seconds. Carriers pay a bounty per bound policy.
why_now: California's rewritten rulebook took effect in 2026 while regulator disclosure stayed opaque, so the information gap is largest now.
revenue_model: $99-249/month per agent, plus $75-200 carrier bounties per bound policy.
non_obvious_insight: Headlines say California is broken, but reality is a patchwork flipping ZIP by ZIP. Carriers with quota obligations are price-insensitive buyers of distribution, and agents are blind to them.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 independent agencies in wildfire-adjacent counties to a shared outcome log (a form and spreadsheet is enough). Publish a weekly 'who is writing' report and start charging at week four.

title: Concession-Adjusted Comps for Appraisers
one_liner: A browser tool that reconstructs what homes really sold for after seller credits and buydowns, so appraisers, lenders and AVMs stop valuing collateral off gross headline prices.
customer: Independent residential appraisers and small appraisal firms in high-concession metros (Atlanta, Austin, Dallas, Phoenix, Florida) first; then appraisal management companies, HELOC/home-equity lenders and AVM vendors.
problem: Redfin reports 44.7% of Aug 2026 sales carried seller concessions (Atlanta 72.8%) while national price indices still show +3.7% YoY. The recorded price is gross; the credit or rate buydown lives in MLS remarks, agent notes and the Closing Disclosure. Appraisers are expected to adjust comps for concessions but have no reliable data, so they burn hours phoning agents, and collateral values drift above true net prices.
solution: A Chrome/desktop add-on that runs inside the appraiser's own MLS session. It uses LLM extraction over listing remarks, price history and agent notes to estimate concession type and dollar value (closing-cost credit, 2-1 buydown cost, permanent points), asks the appraiser to confirm with a one-click agent email, and writes a supported adjustment into the sales-comparison grid. Confirmed records build a cooperative net-price database, later licensed as an index and API.
why_now: Record concession share with 30-year rates near 7.5% has made seller-funded buydowns a de facto financing product. Structured appraisal reporting makes concession fields explicit, and LLMs only recently became reliable at parsing messy MLS remarks.
revenue_model: $49-79 per appraiser seat per month; site licenses for AMCs and lenders; net-price index and API licensed to AVM vendors and home-equity portfolios ($0.10-0.50 per lookup or an annual data license).
non_obvious_insight: Sellers defend the headline price and negotiate the credit, so the true markdown is invisible in every public index and owned by nobody. Appraisers feel this pain daily, which gives a labeled, growing dataset for free and a wedge into lenders whose collateral models are quietly overstated.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 appraisers from state appraiser groups in Atlanta and Austin. Ship a remarks-parsing concession worksheet as an MVP with a 2-week trial, then charge $49 per month. Publish a monthly 'net vs recorded price' note for five metros to get press and lender attention. Stay within each appraiser's own MLS license and do no bulk scraping.

title: Executive Physicals for Union Trades Members
one_liner: Mobile 'Physical Days' at union halls and apprenticeship centers that give tradespeople the CEO-style cardiometabolic checkup, sold to the multiemployer health funds that pay their claims.
customer: Trustees and administrators of Taft-Hartley multiemployer health and welfare funds (building trades, Teamsters, food and commercial workers) and self-insured municipal and transit plans. First buyer: the fund of a 2,000-member electricians' or pipefitters' local.
problem: Workers 45-64 in the trades carry high rates of hypertension, sleep apnea, hearing loss, silica or dust lung exposure and undetected heart disease, yet they work 6am shifts and cannot make weekday clinic hours. Funds face rising costs (employers say GLP-1 drug costs loom large in the 2026 Business Group on Health survey) but their prevention is a voucher for an annual physical with low uptake. Corporate wellness vendors are built for white-collar campuses, not job sites.
solution: A 45-minute station circuit at the union hall or training center: validated blood pressure, fingerstick lipids and A1c (ApoB by send-out), single-lead ECG for atrial fibrillation, spirometry for dusty trades, audiogram, a STOP-BANG screen with a hand-off home sleep test, grip and gait, and FIT kits. A physician or NP reviews results the same day. Intermediate-risk members get a pre-booked $75-150 coronary calcium scan at a partner imaging center, and members with findings get a fast lane through a care navigator. Occupation-specific add-ons: sleep apnea for drivers, hearing and silica for construction. Fixed-fee pricing with no referral kickbacks.
why_now: GLP-1 spending has made plan sponsors receptive to prevention offsets. Point-of-care devices are now small and cheap enough to run a full circuit from two suitcases. Skilled-trades labor is aging and scarce, so trustees have a genuine interest in keeping members working and healthy longer.
revenue_model: $150-250 per participant paid by the fund, quarterly repeat days, plus optional shared-savings on downstream claims after the first year; add-on family-member days for spouses.
non_obvious_insight: Unions and multiemployer funds are the last pooled buyer with a 30-year time horizon on each member, so they are among the few payers who can actually capture the return on prevention (a corporate employer loses the employee after three years). Trustees are elected by the workers, so 'the same physical executives pay $5,000 for' is politically powerful. Elite prevention has to be sold where the payer keeps the member long enough to profit.
first_30_days: Get an introduction through an apprenticeship training center director or a local business manager. Offer a free or at-cost Physical Day for 40 members, staffed by a physician partner and two techs (roughly $6k in costs). Collect anonymized data on undiagnosed hypertension, high ApoB, apnea risk and hearing loss. Bring a one-page summary to the trustees at their next quarterly meeting comparing the cost of 30 physicals to one avoided cardiac event. Aim to sign a recurring contract within 4-5 months.
